newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court rules for workers on benefits case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court rules for workers on benefits case.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled Monday that a federal pension law makes it illegal for an employer to fire employees and contract out their jobs to another company just to cut their benefits.

The ruling was a victory for the U.S. Justice and Labor department, which argued that the pension law prohibits the firing of employees for the purpose of interfering with their rights under an employee welfare benefit plan.

The case involved a 1974 federal law that governs employee pension and benefit plans. The law requires pension benefits to be vested within five years, which means a worker cannot be forced to give up those benefits.
The law allows employers to reduce or cancel benefits at any time. But it bars employers from firing or discriminating against workers in an effort to interfere with their right to collect benefits.

The case involved a lawsuit by a group of former employees in Los Angeles of The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway Co. They sued after the railroad in 1990 shifted their jobs to another company, charging it was aimed at depriving them of various benefits.
A federal judge and a U.S. appeals court ruled against the workers, but the high court in an opinion by Justice Sandra Day O'Connor reinstated their claims, sending the case back for more hearings.
